text: Early treatment in #Alzheimer's has tremendous social value. Early treatment can reduce the years spent with severe dementia by about one-third — which means almost $140,000 in benefits for each patient.

As an academic researcher, there is perhaps nothing more satisfying than seeing literal decades of research translate into bold policy action with the stroke of a pen… It's a historic milestone for public health, but there is more work to address the obesity crisis.

USC Schaeffer Institute hosted CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz and his senior team. Our discussion focused on how rigorous research can help align healthcare resources with patient needs — including how GLP-1 therapies reduce the burden of obesity and diabetes, and overcoming the policy challenges around access and affordability.

The USC Schaeffer Institute was honored to host National Institutes of Health and Gates Foundation leadership at USC's capital campus. The goal? How to advance research and policy to make continued progress alleviating diseases like Alzheimer's and HIV.

CMS announced a voluntary model to expand access to GLP-1s. USC Schaeffer research has shown that this coverage will be one of the public sector's best investments — social returns of 13% or more, likely above 16% now that prices are lower. An easy investment decision for states, and hopefully for Part D plans.

Medicare announced the negotiated prices under the IRA. “Negotiated” is a misnomer — really it's prices set by government fiat. Direct-to-consumer prices are set in a competitive marketplace; that is why we don't read stories about being disappointed about the price of an iPhone. More in my letter to the Wall Street Journal.

Tying US drug prices to other, mainly dysfunctional foreign markets makes little economic sense. At ISPOR's annual meeting, USC Schaeffer scholars led key conversations on MFN, health technology assessment, and the future of US drug policy.
Here is a plan that will cover all Americans without increasing costs. The key is recognizing we don't need to subsidize excessive amounts of insurance.
